What are bias and variance?

Simple explanation: Bias is the error from a model being too simple, so it misses the real pattern. Variance is the error from a model being too sensitive to the particular training data. High bias leads to underfitting and high variance leads to overfitting.
Example: An archer's arrows all land to the left of the target: that is high bias. The arrows land all over the place: that is high variance.
Check yourself: Which describes a very deep decision tree better: high bias or high variance?

Why do we split data into train and test sets?

Simple explanation: We keep part of the data hidden from the model during training. The training set is used to learn, and the test set is used afterwards to check how the model performs on data it has never seen.
Example: A teacher solves some problems in class (training) and gives different problems in the exam (test). If the exam repeats the class problems, the score tells you nothing about real understanding.
Check yourself: What could go wrong if we evaluated the model on the same data it trained on?
How does this connect to cross-validation?

Simple explanation: Cross-validation repeats the train/test idea several times. The data is cut into folds, and each fold takes a turn as the test set while the others train the model.
Example: Instead of one exam, you take five small exams and average the results, so one lucky or unlucky exam cannot fool you.
Check yourself: Why is the average of five exams more trustworthy than a single exam?

Check yourself: Does feeling only the local slope guarantee reaching the deepest valley?
